messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 72
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Refugee Aid Worker
  trauma_type: Terrorism
  pcl5: 53

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Self-Blame: repeatedly blame myself for what happened, Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle, Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation
  Threat: Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Minh was sixty-eight when the attack happened, though it sometimes felt as though it had happened yesterday, or to someone else entirely. For thirty years he had worked as a refugee aid worker, mostly in camps along the Thai–Myanmar border, coordinating food distribution and shelter. He had seen hardship, had learned to read the tension in a crowd, to tell when a rumour or a shortage might tip into violence. But what came that afternoon was not a slow escalation. A convoy of supply trucks was stopped at a checkpoint near a camp he knew well, and Minh was in the lead vehicle. The explosion—a car bomb, they later said—tore through the first two trucks. The noise was immense, a pressure that seemed to push through his ears and into his skull, and then a ringing that swallowed everything. He remembered the heat on his face, the smell of diesel and burnt rubber, and the wet, red mess that had been the driver beside him. He could not move his legs at first, though they were not injured. The images stayed: the twisted metal, the dust, a single sandal lying thirty feet away. He could hear, in his mind, a woman screaming—a high, thin sound that did not stop until someone pulled him away.

In the weeks afterward, he told himself he was fine. He had survived. He could replay the event like a film, but it felt distant, as though it had happened to a character in a story. That sense of unreality was almost a comfort at first. He did not tell his wife, Linh, how often he saw the driver’s face when he closed his eyes. The images came uninvited: the flash of the blast, the metal folding, the dust cloud. And sometimes, in the quiet of the night, he heard the scream again—not as a memory but as if it were happening in the next room, a sound that made his body go rigid before his mind caught up.

He stopped driving. It had not been a conscious decision. The first time he got behind the wheel after the attack, his heart began to pound, his hands grew slick, and he had to pull over before he had gone a block. Being a passenger was no better; every turn, every sudden stop, every distant horn sent a jolt through him. He started walking everywhere, or asking Linh to drive him, and he felt a dull shame each time he gave an excuse. At work, he had always prided himself on his calmness during negotiations, his ability to sit with hostile officials and find common ground. Now he found himself avoiding meetings, delegating difficult conversations. If a colleague raised a voice or challenged a decision, Minh’s chest tightened and he heard himself agreeing just to end it. He became certain that any disagreement could spiral into something worse—irrational, he knew, but the feeling was as real as the pain in his back.

At home, he felt safe only in the armchair in the corner of the bedroom, facing the door. The living room, with its large windows, made him uneasy. He could not sit with his back to the door in a restaurant; he had stopped going to any public place without Linh. Ordinary sounds—a car backfiring, a dropped pan, the slam of a neighbour’s door—made him jump as if a bomb had gone off. He was always scanning, always listening, his body braced for a threat that never came. Over time, his world shrank to the bedroom, the kitchen at certain hours, the short walk to the corner store if it was quiet. He ruminated endlessly on the attack, turning over the same questions: *If I had suggested a different route, if I had delayed the convoy by ten minutes…* He blamed himself, even though he knew, with the part of his mind that still reasoned, that he could not have known. The self-blame became a loop, a way of staying close to the event, of keeping it real when the memory itself felt like a nightmare that someone else had dreamed.

What finally brought him to the clinic was his grandson’s fourth birthday party. Minh had promised to come, but the night before he lay awake imagining the noise, the crowd, the impossibility of leaving if he needed to. He called in the morning and said he was unwell. Linh did not argue, but her silence said everything. That afternoon he sat in his armchair and wept. He was seventy-two years old, and he could not go to a birthday party. He had been a man who had crossed borders under fire, and now a balloon bursting would make him shake for an hour. He came to therapy not because he expected to be cured, but because he was desperate for the world to feel even a little bit less dangerous. He was most afraid that the terror would never loosen its grip, that he would spend whatever years he had left in that armchair. And he was hoping, in a quiet way he did not dare to voice, that he might one day drive himself to see his grandson.
